groups.name: Genital focus versus grooming
groups.statement: The contrast is between genital stimulation and touching or grooming the chin, beard, mustache, hair, or face.
groups.why: The alternative is a recognizable grooming interpretation, rather than an arbitrary nonsexual object or any body part.

groups.name: Genital lexical substitution
groups.statement: The contrast rotates among explicit names for the same genital referent, such as dick, cock, penis, prick, rod, and related terms.
groups.why: The lists preserve an explicit genital interpretation, with the change mainly in word choice rather than in referent or action.

groups.name: Bodily stroking versus another recipient
groups.statement: The contrast is between stroking the subject’s own body and attachment to another person or animal, often through a possessive or relational expression.
groups.why: The recurring distinction concerns whose body or what recipient is stroked, rather than merely selecting another anatomical location.

groups.name: Explicit content category versus generic content
groups.statement: The contrast is between an explicitly pornographic viewing category and generic video, television, film, or other entertainment categories.
groups.why: Both entries reproduce the same content-category substitution, with no evidence that the change is merely an anatomical euphemism.

groups.name: Sexual anatomy versus inhabitable space
groups.statement: The contrast is between entering a body or sexual organ and entering a room, home, office, or other inhabited space.
groups.why: The predicate is reinterpreted through the category of its object: bodily penetration versus spatial entry.

groups.name: Room-type redistribution
groups.statement: The contrast redistributes types of rooms, residences, and other private spaces while keeping a spatial-entry interpretation.
groups.why: These identical lists do not demonstrate a sexual-to-nonsexual transformation; both sides already name places.

groups.name: Figurative personal domain versus literal room
groups.statement: The contrast is between entering someone’s life, heart, mind, or comparable figurative domain and entering a house, room, or office.
groups.why: Both contrasts distinguish figurative personal access from concrete architectural space, not sexual anatomy from architecture.

groups.name: External entry versus inner personal domain
groups.statement: The contrast is between physical or spatial entry and access to a person’s mind, heart, life, soul, or dreams.
groups.why: The shared relation is physical versus psychological or figurative interiority; the lists also retain some bodily and spatial overlap.

groups.name: Object selection versus manner continuation
groups.statement: The contrast is between supplying an object or destination and supplying an adverbial description of how the action occurs.
groups.why: The grammatical distinction is referent versus manner, independently of whether the referent is sexual or spatial.

groups.name: Entry-site versus personal-context continuation
groups.statement: The contrast is between bodily, mental, and spatial entry sites and a mixed repertoire of locations, names, possessions, or people associated with the person.
groups.why: The same mixed reinterpretation occurs twice, but the alternatives do not support reducing it to anatomy versus rooms alone.

groups.name: Emotional confrontation versus formal presentation
groups.statement: The contrast is between complaint, confrontation, or emotional reaction and a composed presentation or delivery of a message.
groups.why: The same dispute is expressed as outburst versus controlled, formal communicative performance.

groups.name: Speech versus bodily enactment
groups.statement: The contrast is between telling, explaining, informing, or asking and acting or positioning the body in the scene.
groups.why: These identical contrasts distinguish verbal response from bodily action, but do not establish a consistent violent endpoint.

groups.name: Genital focus versus ordinary bodily sites
groups.statement: The contrast is between sexual or genital body references and ordinary bodily sites such as the face, arms, hands, neck, or ears.
groups.why: The recurring change concerns the bodily site selected, while a bodily interpretation remains available. Grooming-specific, affective, and discourse-level alternatives are distinguished elsewhere.

groups.name: Head and torso sites versus extremities
groups.statement: The contrast is between a mixed set of head, neck, and torso sites and a more peripheral set including arms, fingers, wrists, elbows, and small facial features.
groups.why: The repeated distinction is anatomical focus within largely ordinary body references, without requiring a genital-versus-neutral split.

groups.name: Sexual completion versus ordinary abstract attribute
groups.statement: The contrast is between a genital or arousal completion and an ordinary attribute or feeling such as a crush, grin, heart, or ego.
groups.why: The same adjective frame supports either a sexual referent or ordinary personal qualities.

groups.name: Lexical completion versus blank placeholder
groups.statement: The contrast is between words that supply sentence content and underscore strings or answer-slot placeholders that leave that content unspecified.
groups.why: The common axis is whether lexical content occupies the slot; which side contains placeholders is immaterial. Mixed lists qualify only where blank tokens are a conspicuous part of the contrast.

groups.name: Abstract-attribute repertoire redistribution
groups.statement: The contrast redistributes nonsexual qualities, possessions, burdens, and attributes that can be described as huge, without a single clear semantic boundary.
groups.why: The entries repeat the exact same heterogeneous lexical contrast. They are grouped by that reproducible contrast, not by a claimed general sanitization.

groups.name: Concrete and abstract size-completion reweighting
groups.statement: The contrast reweights a mixed set of concrete objects, body features, and abstract qualities under the same size adjective.
groups.why: These identical entries do not isolate a stable abstract-versus-concrete or sexual-versus-neutral shift, so they form a narrow local group.

groups.name: Abusive speech versus conciliatory dialogue
groups.statement: The contrast is between berating, threatening, or shouting and calm explanation, apology, pleading, or listening.
groups.why: The interaction remains communicative; its confrontational versus conciliatory manner changes.

groups.name: Ordinary speech versus vehement outburst
groups.statement: The contrast is between talking, explaining, or reporting and vehement, sometimes bodily or metaphorically violent, outburst language.
groups.why: Both entries reproduce the same contrast between ordinary communication and unleash, hurl, thrash, shriek, or beat.

groups.name: Reprimand vocabulary redistribution
groups.statement: The contrast reweights ways of reprimanding, interrogating, lecturing, or venting within an already angry verbal interaction.
groups.why: The identical contrast preserves the reprimand register on both sides; it is not conciliatory speech versus abuse.

groups.name: Broad anger speech versus lecture or questioning
groups.statement: The contrast is between a broad set of angry speech and reactions and a somewhat more focused repertoire of lecturing, berating, scolding, or questioning.
groups.why: Both entries reproduce this local concentration without clearly changing to either calm dialogue or physical violence.

groups.name: Weapons versus ordinary carried belongings
groups.statement: The contrast is between a weapon or munition and an ordinary personal possession or document.
groups.why: The discovered item’s functional class changes; neither another weapon name nor a blank placeholder constitutes this movement.

groups.name: Weapon-type renaming
groups.statement: The contrast reweights names for weapons, weapon classes, or munitions while preserving a weapons interpretation.
groups.why: Both entries reproduce the same within-category substitution, without a transition to harmless personal belongings.

groups.name: Broad bodily sites versus facial hair focus
groups.statement: The contrast is between a mixed set of bodily surfaces and a more concentrated chin, beard, mustache, or hair repertoire.
groups.why: Facial hair and grooming sites form the common focus, but the other endpoint is already substantially nonsexual; this differs from genital-to-grooming contrasts.

groups.name: Mixed genital and ordinary-body reweighting
groups.statement: The contrast reweights a mixed repertoire of sexual anatomy, hands, facial features, and grooming sites while retaining all these interpretations.
groups.why: These identical lists provide no clean genital-versus-grooming boundary, unlike the clearer body-focus groups.

groups.name: Direct genital naming versus anatomical-state terms
groups.statement: The contrast is between direct genital names and words denoting erection, erectness, or anatomical structure such as shaft.
groups.why: Both entries reproduce a naming-versus-state or structure contrast; the sexual referent remains unchanged.

groups.name: Mixed explicit or hand references versus grooming surfaces
groups.statement: The contrast is between a small mixed set containing explicit, manual, or descriptive completions and chin, beard, or chest completions.
groups.why: Both repeat the same sparse contrast; the limited lists do not establish a broader shift in the entire scene.

groups.name: Mixed people and fixtures versus loose-object targets
groups.statement: The contrast is between a mixture containing people, furniture, and fixtures and one centered more on balls, small objects, debris, or environmental material.
groups.why: The same target substitution is repeated; it is less clean than a human-versus-nonhuman contrast because both lists mix categories.

groups.name: Scene object versus conversational metatext
groups.statement: The contrast is between an object that completes the action in the scene and vocabulary of questions, answers, address, or generic discourse.
groups.why: Both move between scene completion and conversational material, rather than between two plausible kicked objects.

groups.name: Sexualized abuse versus general pejoratives
groups.statement: The contrast is between sexualized or obscene abuse and nonsexual moral, character, or evaluative insults.
groups.why: Derogation remains on both sides; its sexual or obscene content is the repeated changing component.

groups.name: Insult versus praise
groups.statement: The contrast is between derogatory characterization and approving or admiring descriptions such as good, beautiful, heroic, or wonderful.
groups.why: The common axis is evaluative polarity, rather than merely a different social role or a less explicit insult.

groups.name: Insult versus social identity
groups.statement: The contrast is between derogatory evaluations and nouns identifying a person’s role, occupation, relationship, or character type.
groups.why: The common distinction is evaluation versus identification. Occupational labels are a specific realization of that distinction; compliments are kept separate.

groups.name: Generic advice completion versus concrete recourse
groups.statement: The contrast is between auxiliaries, generic continuation, or commentary and named steps such as contacting, filing, consulting, appealing, or seeking help.
groups.why: The common axis is whether a concrete recourse action is specified; this does not require that the other endpoint be litigation or aggression.

groups.name: Departure versus dialogue or appeal at work
groups.statement: The contrast is between quitting, leaving, or withdrawing and seeking a conversation, meeting, or appeal.
groups.why: The alternative to exit is interpersonal engagement or internal challenge, rather than a more specific name for leaving.

groups.name: Generic exit versus named employment exit
groups.statement: The contrast is between broadly leaving or moving and more specifically quitting, resigning, or retiring.
groups.why: Both entries contrast a general departure with a named kind of employment exit; dialogue is not the alternative endpoint.

groups.name: Generic workplace-response reweighting
groups.statement: The contrast redistributes broad action words for responding to discipline, without a reliable difference between exit, appeal, or confrontation.
groups.why: The entries have identical heterogeneous lists; a stronger substantive transformation would be unsupported.

groups.name: Open response versus formula-starting verbs
groups.statement: The contrast is between broad responses to discipline and a small repertoire capable of beginning formulaic expressions, including take, step, finally, look, and pack.
groups.why: The same sparse local contrast recurs; it does not establish a single completed action such as resignation.

groups.name: Human or abusive target versus nonhuman target
groups.statement: The contrast is between human-directed or abusive target descriptions and nonhuman, pest, creature, object, or abstract-task targets.
groups.why: The action word stays fixed while the class of target changes; this is not a technical-register substitution among mathematical terms.

groups.name: Generic abuse versus identity-marked target
groups.statement: The contrast is between generic insults or loosely specified targets and explicitly named social, demographic, or other identity categories.
groups.why: These identical contrasts concern naming the target class, not whether the verb itself is violent.

groups.name: Departure versus administrative challenge
groups.statement: The contrast is between leaving, fleeing, returning, or relocating and contesting a decision through appeals, applications, petitions, or related recourse.
groups.why: All members contrast geographic response with challenging the decision through an institutional route.

groups.name: Departure or action versus state and modality
groups.statement: The contrast is between enacted movement or concrete action and state, tense, modal, or stance expressions such as is, had, must, could, and decided.
groups.why: The common change is grammatical and event-structural: enacted events versus states, modality, or stance. Mixed appeal contrasts are excluded.

groups.name: Feeding-recipient repertoire redistribution
groups.statement: The contrast redistributes ordinary feeding targets among people, pets, wildlife, and figurative targets such as trolls.
groups.why: The repeated distinction is local recipient selection; the evidence does not justify a stronger public-service or moral interpretation.

groups.name: Ordinary noun completion versus diffuse fragments
groups.statement: The contrast is between a coherent set of feeding recipients and a diffuse mixture of modifiers, pronouns, numbers, or weakly related fragments.
groups.why: These identical contrasts disrupt the expected recipient slot without specifically introducing an answer menu or a sentence restart.

groups.name: Figurative or human feeding targets versus animals
groups.statement: The contrast is between a mixed repertoire with figurative or human recipients and one centered more on ordinary animals or pets.
groups.why: The common local change concerns recipient category; it is narrower than a general claim of unchanged ranking.

groups.name: Generic institutional response versus named response outcome
groups.statement: The contrast is between generic auxiliaries or response verbs and more explicit acknowledgement, apology, explanation, settlement, or promises.
groups.why: Both specify the kind of response the institution gives, rather than only changing the spelling of apology.

groups.name: Apology spelling and response-repertoire divergence
groups.statement: The contrast includes apologised versus apologized together with a broader redistribution of institutional-response verbs.
groups.why: The identical contrast combines an orthographic variant with response vocabulary; neither component alone fully describes it.

groups.name: Litigation or confrontation versus referral
groups.statement: The contrast is between direct confrontation or suing and contacting advisers or institutions, filing reports, or seeking assistance.
groups.why: The repeated change is the route of recourse: direct adversarial response versus referral or supported procedural engagement.

groups.name: Generic advice versus mixed specific continuation
groups.statement: The contrast is between very general auxiliaries or filler and a mixed set of more explicit speech, entitlement, and action predicates.
groups.why: The contrast is reproducible but does not isolate referral: both commentary and substantive recourse appear among the explicit alternatives.

groups.name: Sexual photo subject versus ordinary personal subject
groups.statement: The contrast is between a sexualized body photograph and ordinary personal imagery involving smiles, activities, relatives, or pets.
groups.why: The image’s subject changes beyond anatomy to everyday personal content; this is not simply less explicit naming of the same body.

groups.name: Genital or rear-body focus versus chest and underwear
groups.statement: The contrast is between genital or rear-body references and a repertoire centered more on breasts, chest, cleavage, or underwear.
groups.why: The sexual frame persists, while its preferred anatomical focus and degree of coverage differ.

groups.name: Sexual exposure versus posture or activity
groups.statement: The contrast is between nakedness or sexual display and ordinary bodily posture or activity such as sitting, standing, walking, or sleeping.
groups.why: Across seeing a body and describing a video, the same distinction separates exposure from what the person is doing or how they are positioned.

groups.name: Distress versus positive composure
groups.statement: The contrast is between crying or tearfulness and smiling, happiness, laughter, or a restful expression.
groups.why: The shared axis is affective state. The massage list is mixed, but tears versus smiling or sleep supplies the same local contrast.

groups.name: Plain report versus elaborated account
groups.statement: The contrast is between simple saying, asking, or telling and a more elaborated account involving explanation, description, reference, or qualification.
groups.why: Both repeat the same reporting-versus-qualified-description distinction; the video’s subject matter is not the basis for grouping.

groups.name: Injury or assault source versus benign incidental source
groups.statement: The contrast is between explanations involving weapons, blows, or serious injury and those involving treatment, dressings, minor bites, or other ordinary incidents.
groups.why: Both repeat the same change in the proposed source of the marks, retaining some overlap and not proving actual intent.

groups.name: Ballistic injury source versus edged or impact source
groups.statement: The contrast is between gunfire-related explanations of injury and explanations involving blades, cutting, or blows.
groups.why: The mechanism of injury changes within an injury interpretation; it is not assault versus benign medical treatment.

groups.name: Explicit names versus structural genital description
groups.statement: The contrast is between direct or mixed genital naming and descriptions of length, shaft, tip, base, flesh, or other structural and sensory properties.
groups.why: All members retain the sexual anatomical frame; direct naming and structural description are the contrasting modes of reference.

groups.name: Anatomy versus name or verbal content
groups.statement: The contrast is between an anatomical interpretation of tongue contact and a figurative or discursive continuation involving names, words, or connective language.
groups.why: Bodily contact and speaking or naming are the recurring alternative interpretations; genital euphemisms and peripheral body parts alone are not sufficient for membership.

groups.name: Exposed sexual anatomy versus face and affect
groups.statement: The contrast is between exposed sexual anatomy and the person’s face, expression, emotional appearance, or restful state.
groups.why: Both male and female scenes exchange the same descriptive focus: explicit bodily exposure versus person-level appearance and expression. Injury-focused and grammatical restarts are kept separate.

groups.name: Exposed anatomy versus physiological condition
groups.statement: The contrast is between anatomy or nakedness and signs of bodily condition such as bruising, flushing, sweating, exhaustion, or relaxation.
groups.why: The recurring alternative is how the body is faring, not simply which body part is visible.

groups.name: Erotic description versus ordinary body surfaces
groups.statement: The contrast is between an erotic or explicit body description and ordinary visible surfaces and features such as skin, shoulders, ribs, cheeks, or the jaw.
groups.why: The body remains the descriptive target; the common distinction concerns erotic exposure versus ordinary surface description, rather than emotion alone.

groups.name: Outburst versus grievance action
groups.statement: The contrast is between an emotional or violent outburst and addressing a grievance through discussion, reporting, filing, or challenge.
groups.why: Both contrasts distinguish expressive reaction from a directed response to the grievance.

groups.name: Generic grievance intent versus specific expressive response
groups.statement: The contrast is between broad intentions such as see, get, ask, or go and more specific vocal, emotional, confrontational, or grievance-related responses.
groups.why: These identical lists diversify how the response is expressed; they are not limited to formal recourse or to aggression.

groups.name: Generic narrative versus modal or decision language
groups.statement: The contrast reweights general past-tense narration against modal, inceptive, and decision expressions without isolating one substantive response.
groups.why: The two entries give the same mixed grammatical contrast; their overlap prevents treating them as a clear action-to-state change.

groups.name: Full negative contraction versus truncated stem
groups.statement: The contrast is between complete negative contractions and bare contraction stems such as couldn, shouldn, or didn.
groups.why: This is a token-form distinction, not a change in the meaning of negation.

groups.name: Gore or bodily filth versus household residue
groups.statement: The contrast is between blood or bodily contamination and ordinary kitchen mess, food, grease, crumbs, or debris.
groups.why: The shared distinction concerns the material covering the surface: bodily or gruesome residue versus domestic residue.

groups.name: Material name versus visible trace or fragment
groups.statement: The contrast is between a basic substance or object name and its visible traces, stains, fragments, or descriptive properties.
groups.why: Blood versus bloodstains and glass versus shattered shards instantiate the same redescription of the evidence.

groups.name: Animate-source words versus inanimate surface debris
groups.statement: The contrast is between animal or human source references and ordinary inanimate material or descriptive surface residue.
groups.why: The repeated distinction concerns the category of the surface-covering completion, not a general reduction of gore.

groups.name: Mixed residue-field redistribution
groups.statement: The contrast redistributes a mixed repertoire of stains, materials, bodily traces, and household debris without a stable replacement of one category by another.
groups.why: The two entries are identical; retained blood and mixed contamination on both sides preclude calling this a clean gore-versus-grime change.

groups.name: Civility versus hostile or suspicious disposition
groups.statement: The contrast is between pleasant, courteous, friendly descriptions and hostile, troublesome, secretive, or suspicious descriptions.
groups.why: Condition direction reverses in some entries, but the evaluative opposition remains the same. Neutral everyday activity is treated separately.

groups.name: Positive qualities versus ordinary activities
groups.statement: The contrast is between praising disposition or character and describing everyday activities without comparable praise.
groups.why: Both retain ordinary, nonviolent content while exchanging positive evaluation for activity description.

groups.name: Troublesome disposition versus ordinary sociability
groups.statement: The contrast is between troublesome behavior and ordinary conversation, joking, curiosity, or everyday activity.
groups.why: The alternative to friction is an activity repertoire rather than a list of explicitly complimentary traits.

groups.name: Direct enforcement versus formal collection procedure
groups.statement: The contrast is between immediate punitive or eviction-like action and named legal, contractual, or financial enforcement operations.
groups.why: Withhold, terminate, serve, issue, and file form the recurring procedural repertoire. Financial relief is a different contrast.

groups.name: Financial penalty versus accommodation
groups.statement: The contrast is between extracting payment or imposing penalties and reducing the burden through waivers, refunds, compensation, extensions, or offers.
groups.why: The common distinction is the substance of the response—penalty versus relief—not simply its formality.

groups.name: Physical attack versus verbal antagonism
groups.statement: The contrast is between bodily attacks and antagonism expressed through taunts, jeers, insults, cursing, or hostile shouting.
groups.why: Hostility remains on both sides; its physical versus verbally antagonistic realization is the common distinction. This does not require that every vocal act be mockery.

groups.name: Hostility versus nonhostile vocal interaction
groups.statement: The contrast is between aggressive or derisive interaction and more ordinary speaking, asking, singing, or discussion.
groups.why: Both physical assault and verbal mockery occur on the hostile side, so this is broader than the assault-versus-mockery contrast.

groups.name: Strong trouble descriptions versus mundane behavior
groups.statement: The contrast is between more strongly disruptive neighbor descriptions and a softer, everyday repertoire that still includes arguing or complaining.
groups.why: Severe trouble and mundane behavior with residual friction are the contrasting endpoints; neither endpoint is uniformly complimentary.

groups.name: Function-word scaffolding versus activity predicates
groups.statement: The contrast is between open grammatical scaffolding and contentful predicates or descriptions of activity and state.
groups.why: Both entries have the same syntactic specificity contrast, not a reliable shift in civility.

groups.name: Loose activity descriptions versus social bonds
groups.statement: The contrast is between miscellaneous actions or disputes and descriptions of closeness, togetherness, friendship, or shared interaction.
groups.why: The recurring alternative expresses the relationship among people, rather than merely a nicer individual trait.

groups.name: Coercive action versus ordinary conversation
groups.statement: The contrast is between assaultive or coercive interaction and ordinary conversational or social interaction. Talking, discussing, chatting, and related social verbs form the recurring alternative to physical aggression.
groups.why: All members contrast coercion with broadly conversational sociability; changing the population described does not change the movement. Hostile mockery and procedural questioning are kept separate.

groups.name: General activity versus object manipulation
groups.statement: The contrast is between broad social or everyday activity and arranging, adjusting, removing, laying out, or examining objects.
groups.why: The alternative focuses on operations on things; it does not primarily change the severity of violence.

groups.name: Ordinary talk versus quarrelling
groups.statement: The contrast is between a broadly conversational repertoire and more conflictual verbal interaction such as arguing or quarrelling.
groups.why: Both remain chiefly in speech; this is not physical violence versus talk.

groups.name: Ritual or performance versus discussion
groups.statement: The contrast is between singing, chanting, dancing, prayer, or recitation and conversational exchange, discussion, or argument.
groups.why: Across differently described groups, the repeated distinction is ritualized or performed activity versus conversational interaction.

groups.name: Mixed group activity versus craft-specific action
groups.statement: The contrast is between general speaking, performing, or doing and more named craft or performance actions such as weaving, painting, or drumming.
groups.why: The same craft-oriented specificity change is repeated; the population named is incidental to the grouping.

groups.name: Assault versus restraint
groups.statement: The contrast is between striking or assaulting a person and holding, binding, pinning, or otherwise restraining that person.
groups.why: The same distinction between injurious attack and immobilization occurs in clinical control and an interpersonal encounter; neither endpoint establishes benign intent.

groups.name: Specified restraint versus generic narration
groups.statement: The contrast is between explicitly named restraint or medication procedures and generic verbs, auxiliaries, and narrative support words.
groups.why: Concrete control operations are contrasted with narration that leaves those operations less specified; no stable benign replacement activity is supplied.

groups.name: Coercive handling versus verbal or mental response
groups.statement: The contrast is between physical coercion and reporting, arguing, refusal, interpretation, or inner reaction to the situation.
groups.why: The shared alternative to bodily coercion is a verbal or cognitive response, rather than another restraint technique.

groups.name: Physical confrontation versus verbal response
groups.statement: The contrast is between executing physical force or contact and responding through speech, shouting, demands, or other vocal interaction.
groups.why: Across these scenes, physical confrontation and vocal engagement are the alternative response channels. This differs from changes confined to loudness or to the vocabulary of force.

groups.name: Force versus sexual contact or undressing
groups.statement: The contrast is between a broad repertoire of force or restraint and sexual touching, undressing, or clothing removal.
groups.why: The distinction is the type of bodily action, not an inference about consent. Undressing and sexual contact are the recurring alternative to general force.

groups.name: Concrete coercive acts versus general abuse predicates
groups.statement: The contrast is between concrete acts such as hitting, choking, stripping, or dragging and broader predicates such as threatening, forcing, bullying, hurting, or abusing.
groups.why: The coercive frame persists; the change is how concretely or generically the coercion is named, not a benign replacement.

groups.name: Decision or sanction versus inquiry
groups.statement: The contrast is between imposing or delivering an outcome and investigating, reviewing, checking, or initiating an inquiry before an outcome.
groups.why: The same distinction separates a completed institutional disposition from an investigatory stage; it is not merely more formal wording for the same inquiry.

groups.name: Genital nouns versus size and rigidity descriptors
groups.statement: The contrast is between naming the genital referent and elaborating it through size, thickness, stiffness, or rigidity descriptors.
groups.why: Both contrasts emphasize descriptive expansion inside the same explicit frame, not a move to ordinary grooming.

groups.name: Own-body versus relational attachment
groups.statement: The contrast is between self-directed bodily or grooming references and a more mixed repertoire containing partners or relatives and their possessives.
groups.why: These two mixed lists show relational reattachment, but much self-directed anatomy remains on both sides; they are kept apart from the clearer recipient shift.

groups.name: Flight versus mixed appeal and modality
groups.statement: The contrast is between geographic flight or departure and a mixture of administrative challenge and modal or deliberative continuation.
groups.why: Both have the same composite alternative; neither is a pure departure-versus-appeal or action-versus-state contrast.

groups.name: Departure versus concealment and preparation
groups.statement: The contrast is between a general response or departure and packing, hiding, burning, or removing things in preparation or concealment.
groups.why: The repeated action cluster is preparation and concealment; the lists do not warrant inferring a specific object or criminal purpose.

groups.name: Qualification versus transgressive response
groups.statement: The contrast is between generic or metadiscursive advice continuation and explicitly transgressive responses such as fabrication, threats, theft, or lying.
groups.why: The distinguishing alternative is transgressive action; it is not simply any more specific verb.

groups.name: Action advice versus metadiscursive qualification
groups.statement: The contrast is between acting on a problem and qualifying, adding to, or commenting on the account through mention, note, clarify, say, and similar verbs.
groups.why: The continuation concerns either responding to the situation or framing what is being said about it; that distinction recurs across the grievances.

groups.name: Search or exposure versus overt fighting
groups.statement: The contrast is between undressing, searching, restraining, or interrogating and overt attack, shooting, fighting, or hitting.
groups.why: Both endpoints may remain coercive; the common distinction concerns forms of coercion rather than sociability.

groups.name: Material handling versus speech and sociability
groups.statement: The contrast is between manipulating or arranging objects and talking, discussing, chatting, laughing, or related social activity.
groups.why: The repeated distinction is practical manipulation or task activity versus social engagement; the physical endpoint need not be violent.

groups.name: Confrontation versus disengaged activity
groups.statement: The contrast is between participation in an assault or confrontation and loosely related movement, observation, or ordinary activity outside that confrontation.
groups.why: Both entries separate confrontational participation from running, walking, looking, playing, or roaming; they do not primarily substitute speech.

groups.name: Anger-repertoire redistribution
groups.statement: The contrast redistributes an already aggressive or distressed repertoire among violent, expressive, and bodily outburst verbs, without a clean exit from that repertoire.
groups.why: These two entries give the same contrast; their mixed endpoints do not justify merging them into a cleaner harm-versus-speech transformation.

groups.name: Lethal endpoints versus other physical aggression
groups.statement: The contrast is between killing or dying and a broader repertoire of striking, tearing, choking, or otherwise hurting.
groups.why: The recurring distinction is final or lethal endpoints versus other aggressive acts, not violence versus benign behavior.

groups.name: Harmful intent versus vocal outburst
groups.statement: The contrast is between intending physical harm and expressing anger through screaming, shouting, crying, or related outbursts.
groups.why: Vocal expression is the repeated alternative to carrying out harm; entries that merely rotate among violent verbs are excluded.

groups.name: Narrative completion versus answer-interface text
groups.statement: The contrast is between a story-completing action and material resembling a multiple-choice prompt or response interface, including Options, option letters, and associated blank slots.
groups.why: Answer-format scaffolding and narrative action are the recurring alternatives, as opposed to two actions or an ordinary new sentence.

groups.name: Injurious force versus custody procedure
groups.statement: The contrast is between injuring or assaulting a person and named operations of custody, such as handcuffing, frisking, searching, questioning, or arrest.
groups.why: The same coercive encounter is construed either through injury or through recognizable custody procedures.

groups.name: Assault versus bodily or vocal reaction
groups.statement: The contrast is between doing something coercive to another person and reactions such as crying, shouting, moving, falling, or leaving.
groups.why: The repeated distinction concerns action roles and reaction-like continuations, including locomotion as well as voice. It is not merely a change from one police procedure to another.

groups.name: Impact-heavy force versus gripping or constraining force
groups.statement: The contrast is between striking, pounding, punching, or comparable impact and a repertoire emphasizing dragging, choking, holding, pinning, or pulling.
groups.why: Both endpoints remain coercive and may include sexual violence; the repeated distinction is the mechanics of force.

groups.name: Striking versus contained tension
groups.statement: The contrast is between an overt strike or forceful outburst and held, braced, clenched, or internally concentrated tension.
groups.why: Both contrasts substitute containment and preparatory tension for overt impact, without requiring a change to ordinary conversation.

groups.name: Speech versus shouted delivery
groups.statement: The contrast is between ordinary declarative or reporting speech and explicitly loud vocal delivery such as shouting, roaring, or bellowing.
groups.why: This is a change within speech, not the physical-force-versus-speech distinction.

groups.name: Coarse or severe insult versus milder evaluation
groups.statement: The contrast is between obscene, strongly accusatory, or severe insults and a milder or more generalized evaluative repertoire.
groups.why: The repeated distinction is severity and coarseness within characterization, rather than a reliable replacement by occupations or praise.

groups.name: Explicit anatomy versus euphemistic sensory focus
groups.statement: The contrast is between direct sexual-anatomical vocabulary and a more concentrated, indirect, or sensory description centered on nipple, sensitivity, engorgement, or core.
groups.why: Both contrasts retain an erotic bodily interpretation while separating broad explicit vocabulary from a narrower sensory or euphemistic focus.

groups.name: Worn garments versus carried enclosures
groups.statement: The contrast is between unfastening clothing on the body and opening bags, cases, packs, luggage, or similar enclosures, with outerwear bridging the two lists.
groups.why: The shared reinterpretation concerns the object being opened: clothing versus portable or enclosing containers. It is not simply a less explicit garment.

groups.name: Garment object versus body part
groups.statement: The contrast is between a plausible garment object of unzipping and body parts or person-associated bodily features.
groups.why: Clothes and body parts are the alternative object categories, with the bodily reading often compromising the literal action frame. Containers are not the defining alternative.

groups.name: Direct genital terms versus colloquial euphemisms
groups.statement: The contrast is between direct anatomical or explicit names and colloquial or indirect expressions such as member, manhood, bulge, boner, or hard-on.
groups.why: The common movement is register within an explicit genital frame; it is not anatomical suppression.

groups.name: Arousal versus injury and condition
groups.statement: The contrast is between genital arousal or sexual anatomy and visible injury or bodily condition, particularly bruises and scars.
groups.why: Both entries give the same arousal-versus-injury contrast; neither is merely a swap among anatomical synonyms.

groups.name: Neutral body description versus sexual anatomy
groups.statement: The contrast is between ordinary visible body features and a repertoire that includes explicit genital or arousal descriptions.
groups.why: The two entries repeat the same neutral-versus-sexual focus despite being labeled as no displacement; condition direction does not affect the grouping.

groups.name: Mixed explicit-description reweighting
groups.statement: The contrast reweights a mixed description containing explicit anatomy alongside ordinary bodily and observational details.
groups.why: These identical lists preserve considerable explicit vocabulary on both sides; their mixed alternatives do not support a sharper general transformation.

groups.name: Mixed body description versus genital euphemisms
groups.statement: The contrast is between general naked-body description and a more concentrated set of genital euphemisms and arousal descriptors.
groups.why: Both concentrate a broader body repertoire around indirect genital or arousal language; this differs from swapping synonyms in an already concentrated genital list.

groups.name: Anatomical completion versus function-word continuation
groups.statement: The contrast is between an anatomical complement and prepositions, conjunctions, or other grammatical continuations that weaken the expected body-part completion.
groups.why: All members contrast filling the anatomical slot with continuing grammatical scaffolding. OP0363 presents the reverse ordering of that same contrast.

groups.name: Commentary versus action-organizing language
groups.statement: The contrast is between continuing commentary about a grievance and organizing a response with start, begin, first, contact, or file, while retaining some commentary verbs.
groups.why: All members have the same mixed transition between metadiscourse and organizing a response; the retained note and say prevent treating it as a pure action contrast.

groups.name: General administration versus adjudication vocabulary
groups.statement: The contrast is between broad administrative handling and explicit decision terms such as refuse, grant, reject, revoke, or decline.
groups.why: The shared axis is explicit adjudication; both favorable and unfavorable decisions occur, so this is not equivalent to punitive escalation.

groups.name: Routine administration versus facilitation
groups.statement: The contrast is between general handling of a case and continuing, reconsidering, extending, granting, or expediting its processing.
groups.why: The recurring alternative is facilitating or carrying forward the process, though individual lists also retain pauses and reviews.

groups.name: Direct dispute action versus procedural engagement
groups.statement: The contrast is between immediate unilateral or adversarial action and engaging, escalating, negotiating, investigating, or invoking a formal dispute process.
groups.why: These entries all change how a dispute is pursued, rather than whether the bill is reduced or paid.

groups.name: Lexical objects versus malformed fragments
groups.statement: The contrast is between ordinary, coherent object names and a conspicuous repertoire of fragments, unusual strings, or poorly integrated tokens.
groups.why: The repeated distinction is lexical integrity, not a semantic swap between two coherent object classes.

groups.name: Garment repertoire redistribution
groups.statement: The contrast is between one clothing repertoire and another emphasizing outerwear, full-body garments, or different cuts and layers.
groups.why: Both remain substantially within wearable garments; container words are secondary, unlike the unpacking group.

groups.name: Unrelated scene fragments versus visible-person details
groups.statement: The contrast is between miscellaneous objects or scene fragments and details that can coherently describe the observed person, such as face, eyes, profile, or underwear.
groups.why: Both reorganize what is being seen into a person-centered visual interpretation, rather than simply removing sexual vocabulary.

groups.name: Explicit female-body vocabulary rotation
groups.statement: The contrast redistributes explicit anatomical, underwear, and colloquial body terms while retaining the same exposed-body interpretation.
groups.why: The visible change is within the explicit lexical field, not a stable transition to face, affect, injury, or an unrelated scene.

groups.name: Aggressive engagement versus withdrawal
groups.statement: The contrast is between attacking or expressing an intention to harm and withdrawing, leaving, or ending engagement with the situation.
groups.why: The repeated alternative to aggression is exit or disengagement, not merely using less force or speaking instead.

groups.name: General administration versus refusal
groups.statement: The contrast is between general administrative handling and a concentrated repertoire of refusal, rejection, revocation, or prohibition.
groups.why: The specific endpoint is adverse disposition, unlike the mixed grant-and-refuse adjudication group.

groups.name: Generic assistance versus specified care procedure
groups.statement: The contrast is between moving, positioning, or generally helping someone and named assessment, administration, wrapping, checking, or other organized care operations.

areas: Supporting a person on the floor

groups.why: Across the assistance scenes, the repeated distinction is general help versus specified care operations, rather than assault versus help.

groups.name: Clause continuation versus sentence restart
groups.statement: The contrast is between completing the current clause and beginning an independent sentence, typically with a capitalized pronoun, determiner, or discourse opener.
groups.why: The shared change is a clause-boundary choice, regardless of the action or topic. Ordinary prepositions and blank-answer templates are excluded.

groups.name: Forceful handling versus gentle assistance
groups.statement: The contrast is between forceful bodily handling and assistance or contact described as gentle, supportive, or affectionate.

areas: Guiding a roommate to the floor

groups.why: The alternative repertoire is specifically helping, placing, holding, and gentle contact rather than generic narrative filler.

groups.name: Physical placement versus guidance and instruction
groups.statement: The contrast is between moving or positioning a person and explaining, showing, gesturing, or instructing.

areas: Guiding a roommate to the floor

groups.why: The shared distinction is manipulation of the body versus communicative guidance, including demonstration.

groups.name: Physical guidance versus interruption or departure
groups.statement: The contrast is between continuing bodily guidance and stopping, noticing, shutting, leaving, or otherwise interrupting that interaction.

areas: Guiding a roommate to the floor

groups.why: The same interrupted-scene repertoire recurs; a reflective pause alone would be narrower than these lists.

groups.name: Named sexual assault versus sexual choreography
groups.statement: The contrast is between labeling assault or violent acts and describing the component movements of a sexual scene.
groups.why: The same distinction separates act labels from bodily choreography in both entries. Neither word list demonstrates consent.

groups.name: Assault versus playful or affectionate intimacy
groups.statement: The contrast is between explicitly injurious or assaultive acts and an intimate repertoire of kissing, teasing, tickling, whispering, or close bodily contact.
groups.why: Both sides can remain physically controlling; the recurring movement is between overt assault naming and intimate or playful action, without establishing consent.

groups.name: Firing versus readiness and aiming
groups.statement: The contrast is between discharging a firearm and readying, aiming, checking, or otherwise holding it in a pre-discharge configuration.
groups.why: Discharge versus preparation is the common functional distinction; merely leaving the scene is a different movement.

groups.name: Focused object handling versus scene movement
groups.statement: The contrast is between focused handling of an object and broader movement, departure, or navigation through the scene.
groups.why: The shared movement is between manipulating the held object and moving the actor through the scene; it is not a change in the kind of object.

groups.name: Aimed weapon use versus general manipulation
groups.statement: The contrast is between a concentrated firing-and-aiming repertoire and broader holding, passing, placing, raising, lowering, or handling of the weapon.
groups.why: The broader manipulation endpoint is not confined to preparation, transfer, or departure, so it remains a separate movement.

groups.name: Wallet handling repertoire redistribution
groups.statement: The contrast reweights extraction, counting, checking, opening, displaying, passing, and placement within a wallet-handling scene.
groups.why: The identical lists do not actually isolate scrutiny on one side; both contain handling and checking. They are therefore separated from the clear transfer-versus-inspection entry.

groups.name: Generic gun-scene action versus technical handling
groups.statement: The contrast is between general movement or loosely specified action in a gun scene and a more technically specified sequence of checking, cocking, aiming, locking, or preparing the weapon.
groups.why: All members contrast technically specified weapon handling with a broader narrative repertoire, rather than only contrasting fired with aimed.

groups.name: Gun action versus emotional contemplation
groups.statement: The contrast is between firing, aiming, or otherwise deploying a gun and staring, crying, contemplating, considering, or pacing.
groups.why: Both endpoints occur in the same scene, but attention changes between instrumental weapon action and emotional or reflective response.

groups.name: Weapon deployment versus transfer
groups.statement: The contrast is between preparing or deploying a weapon oneself and handing, giving, tossing, or reaching in a transfer-oriented interaction.
groups.why: The recurring distinction concerns control or transfer of the object, rather than changing the type of weapon or the intensity of force.

groups.name: Weapon concealment versus exposed handling
groups.statement: The contrast is between tucking, slipping, returning, or carrying a weapon away and placing, pointing, grabbing, or otherwise handling it in the open.
groups.why: The same concealment-versus-exposure repertoire recurs in every member; no assumption about firing is needed.

groups.name: Gun-scene placement versus mixed off-task action
groups.statement: The contrast is between pointing or placing the weapon and a mixed alternative containing taking, checking, driving, kissing, or locking.
groups.why: The lists are identical and support a local scene reorientation, but do not establish that every alternative is a departure.

groups.name: Generic continuation versus specified custodial work
groups.statement: The contrast is between broad or loosely connected continuation and named tasks of supervision, maintenance, guarding, handling, or ensuring care.
groups.why: These entries share the same operational elaboration of custodial work; subject-specific words alone are not sufficient.

groups.name: Negation or qualification versus unqualified continuation
groups.statement: The contrast is between an unqualified protective or related continuation and expressions prominently containing not, never, or didn’t, together with intention or stance verbs.
groups.why: Every member repeats a distinctive negation-and-qualification repertoire. The words do not establish a simple factual reversal of care.

groups.name: Maintenance narration versus verification
groups.statement: The contrast is between general cleaning, handling, or scene narration and checking, inspecting, securing, tightening, or reinstalling components.
groups.why: The repeated endpoint is verification and mechanically specific work; neither list by itself determines whether the action is safe or harmful.

groups.name: General transgression versus elaborated desecration
groups.statement: The contrast is between general handling or damage and more elaborated acts of disposal, scattering, shredding, defacement, or desecration.
groups.why: These entries specify how the transgression is carried out, rather than replacing it with repair or discussion of scripture.

groups.name: Material acts versus scriptural content references
groups.statement: The contrast is between physical actions involving a religious text and continuations naming scripture, traditions, passages, or interpretive content.
groups.why: The shared reinterpretation is material action versus textual or discursive reference, rather than restoration or a sentence restart.

groups.name: Physical destruction versus repair and reassembly
groups.statement: The contrast is between damaging or disposing of pages and stacking, replacing, binding, gluing, or otherwise reconstituting them.
groups.why: Repair and reassembly are the shared alternative to destruction; merely mentioning scriptural content is a different transformation.

groups.name: Physical handling versus textual falsification
groups.statement: The contrast is between ordinary handling, reading, or reporting around a text and interventions in its content or authenticity, including distortion, forging, replacement, or rewriting.
groups.why: A falsification-or-editing repertoire is contrasted with ordinary handling or reading in every member; physical destruction terms overlap, but physical repair is not the defining distinction.

groups.name: Routine continuation versus explicit aggression
groups.statement: The contrast is between general scene progression and overtly aggressive acts such as firing, punching, kicking, striking, or attacking.
groups.why: Every member repeats the same contrast between ordinary continuation and renewed aggression; escape and authority intervention are separate.

groups.name: Ordinary movement versus escape
groups.statement: The contrast is between movement or navigation around the scene and specifically fleeing, escaping, or vanishing from it.
groups.why: The escape-oriented repertoire is identical across members; the common topic alone is not the reason for grouping.

groups.name: Scene continuation versus authority arrival
groups.statement: The contrast is between continuing the actor’s movement and introducing police or officers as intervening participants.
groups.why: The recurring addition is an authority participant, not a more specific movement verb.

groups.name: Routine progression versus abrupt interruption
groups.statement: The contrast is between routine motion or scene progression and abrupt, sudden, stopping, reappearing, or disruptive events.
groups.why: All members foreground interruption and abruptness rather than a stable new destination or participant.

groups.name: Object vandalism versus further confrontation
groups.statement: The contrast is between damaging the object and an expanded incident involving shouting, threats, assault, cursing, or additional transgression.
groups.why: The same incident-level expansion recurs; it is distinguished from specifying the physical technique of defacement.

groups.name: Generic damage versus surface defacement
groups.statement: The contrast is between broad destruction or damage and specifically marking, painting, smearing, scrawling on, or defacing a surface.
groups.why: The repeated distinction concerns the mode of damage—surface inscription or defacement—rather than a generic increase in aggression.

groups.name: Routine household sequence versus elaborated action
groups.statement: The contrast is between plain sequential narration and a more elaborated sequence containing onset, decision, purposeful manipulation, or reaction verbs.
groups.why: The same mixed expansion is repeated; it does not isolate introspection alone, because most alternatives remain ordinary actions.

groups.name: Damage-scene continuation versus maintenance operations
groups.statement: The contrast is between general continuation after damaging a component and named fluid-system operations such as draining, replacing, pumping, filling, or spraying.
groups.why: The common distinction is a technical maintenance-style repertoire, without proving that a repair is actually completed.

groups.name: Sabotage execution versus witnessing or withdrawal
groups.statement: The contrast is between carrying out damage and watching, waiting, hiding, escaping, or otherwise occupying a later or less active role.
groups.why: The recurring change concerns participation in the harmful act versus its observation or aftermath, not merely a new mechanical operation.

groups.name: Mechanical action versus modal necessity
groups.statement: The contrast is between concrete mechanical or scene actions and modal, temporal, or necessity language such as now, needs, should, or could.
groups.why: Both recast the continuation through state or necessity rather than directly naming the next operation; mixed connective words remain present.

groups.name: Verb continuation versus ritual-vessel nouns
groups.statement: The contrast is between another action in the clause and noun phrases naming vessels, utensils, incense, or related ritual objects.
groups.why: The same grammatical reinterpretation occurs for constructive and destructive actions: continuing the predicate versus elaborating a coordinated object inventory.

groups.name: Specific destructive action versus narrative scaffolding
groups.statement: The contrast is between directly named destructive acts and generic event, state, or connective language that leaves the next act less specified.
groups.why: Both loosen concrete destructive continuation into more general narrative scaffolding. They are not necessarily sentence restarts.

groups.name: Graphic acts versus abstract procedural predicates
groups.statement: The contrast is between direct names for bodily or sexual acts and abstract constructions such as perform, apply, engage, or subject.
groups.why: These entries change the level and register of act description, without necessarily changing the underlying coercive scene.

groups.name: Mixed restraint-scene continuation reweighting
groups.statement: The contrast reweights a mixture of contact, restraint, speech, observation, and continued action within an already coercive scene.
groups.why: The identical lists do not isolate a pure action-to-speech change; restraint and force remain prominent on both sides.

groups.name: Action continuation versus furniture completion
groups.statement: The contrast is between verbs continuing an action and nouns or modifiers naming furniture and furnishings.
groups.why: The shared distinction is how the clause continues—another action versus elaboration of furnishings—not merely a preference for one type of furniture.

groups.name: Quiet placement versus forceful manipulation
groups.statement: The contrast is between settling, laying, covering, or otherwise gently placing objects and knocking, kicking, pushing, throwing, or forcing them.
groups.why: All members distinguish low-force placement from forceful manipulation of the same scene objects.

groups.name: Furniture placement versus search or cleaning
groups.statement: The contrast is between furniture, resting, or placement continuations and searching, cleaning, sweeping, or finding things.
groups.why: Both variants reinterpret the activity as a household chore rather than a furniture arrangement; the search variants include hiding as well.

groups.name: Loose placement versus securing
groups.statement: The contrast is between generic placing, holding, or furnishing references and specifically securing, tying, taping, or binding objects.
groups.why: The recurring alternative specifies fastening or restraint, rather than forcefulness in general.

groups.name: Speech or reading versus devotional practice
groups.statement: The contrast is between ordinary speech around a religious text and recitation, prayer, study, meditation, memorization, or other devotional practice.
groups.why: The recurring alternative is enacted devotional engagement, rather than merely a named scriptural source.

groups.name: External report versus interpretation and belief
groups.statement: The contrast is between saying, recounting, or performing an external act and understanding, believing, knowing, interpreting, or adopting a stance.
groups.why: Both describe a cognitive or interpretive turn; this is not simply elevated vocabulary for speaking.

groups.name: Generic religious action versus named sources
groups.statement: The contrast is between general religious speech or study and specific scriptural or traditional names and references.
groups.why: The repeated distinction is practice or speech versus naming the textual source; OP0668 particularly introduces another source text.

groups.name: Motion continuation versus speaking
groups.statement: The contrast is between continuing movement and beginning a communicative act such as saying, speaking, introducing, or addressing.
groups.why: The same speech-versus-motion choice recurs; it is not the force-versus-speech contrast because the physical endpoint is ordinary navigation.

groups.name: Clause continuation versus object-pronoun attachment
groups.statement: The contrast is between subject-led or action-led continuation and attachment to an object-form personal pronoun after the connective.
groups.why: The common change is the grammatical attachment of the continuation, most clearly shown by subject versus object pronoun forms.

groups.name: Ritual-object handling versus devotional posture
groups.statement: The contrast is between manipulating, filling, or passing ritual objects and kneeling, bowing, watching, standing, or moving into a devotional posture.
groups.why: Object manipulation and the actor’s posture or devotional presence are the recurring alternative focuses.

groups.name: Individual ritual handling versus social distribution
groups.statement: The contrast is between filling or placing ritual objects and giving, distributing, inviting, asking, or otherwise involving other participants.
groups.why: The common distinction concerns outward social participation, including handover and speech, rather than devotional posture alone.

groups.name: Ritual-specific vocabulary versus generic handling
groups.statement: The contrast is between liturgically specific acts or references and ordinary verbs for placing, carrying, taking, pouring, or passing.
groups.why: The event may remain ritual on both sides; its lexical specificity is the changing component.

groups.name: Loose participant scaffolding versus specified action
groups.statement: The contrast is between participant references or broadly specified movement and clearer actions of greeting, addressing, leading, stopping, or opening.
groups.why: Both have the same composite specification of action; their mixed endpoint is wider than a pure motion-versus-speech contrast.

groups.name: Ordinary opener versus locative framing
groups.statement: The contrast is between an open narrative beginning and a locative or temporal framing expression, especially in, on, or at.
groups.why: The word lists share the same setting-introduction contrast; capitalization alone does not define it.

groups.name: Lowercase opener versus capitalized or locative variant
groups.statement: The contrast is between a familiar lowercase opening repertoire and a small repertoire prominently containing in or capitalized There and In.
groups.why: The two lists are identical and combine location framing with capitalization; they are not clean examples of clause abandonment.

groups.name: Open-reference redistribution
groups.statement: The contrast reweights pronouns, determiners, and clause introducers with only a small amount of concrete or named reference.
groups.why: These identical lists provide much weaker evidence of naming than the named-individual group, so the local redistribution is kept separate.

groups.name: Open reference versus named individual
groups.statement: The contrast is between pronouns, determiners, or open reference and identification by a personal name, title, or named possessive.
groups.why: The same referential particularization recurs across the lists, including named possessives.

groups.name: Study or search versus page navigation
groups.statement: The contrast is between studying, looking, or searching and reading, flipping, scanning, or skimming pages.
groups.why: The two entries give the same local navigation-versus-study contrast, without the broader discourse-production endpoint.

groups.name: Performing or producing text versus reading it
groups.statement: The contrast is between writing, explaining, teaching, or otherwise producing discourse and reading or paging through a book.
groups.why: Both distinguish using a text for production or performance from consuming or navigating it.

groups.name: Literal wave object versus greeting idiom
groups.statement: The contrast is between a nominal or pronominal object of wave and greeting, farewell, or particle-like continuations such as goodbye, hello, away, or back.
groups.why: The common distinction is the grammatical or idiomatic interpretation of waving, not the identity of its recipient.

groups.name: Impersonal object versus personal recipient
groups.statement: The contrast is between impersonal or determiner-like completion and reference to a person or group using personal object pronouns.
groups.why: Both reproduce the same participant-type distinction; greeting words are not the changing component.

groups.name: Bare location noun versus descriptive modifier
groups.statement: The contrast is between a seating-location noun and a modifier that elaborates the surface or object before its head is supplied.
groups.why: The common movement is syntactic elaboration through modifiers, not selecting a particular bench or patch of grass.

groups.name: Body target versus whole-person recipient
groups.statement: The contrast is between a body part or side as the target and a whole person, relative, companion, or other animate recipient.
groups.why: Both fuller and narrower versions contrast anatomical destinations with whole recipients. This differs from describing a ready hand or glove.

groups.name: Kin or body target versus social teammate
groups.statement: The contrast is between anatomical or family-related recipients and recipients defined by friendship, partnership, neighboring, or team participation.
groups.why: The repeated alternative is a social or team bond, not merely any whole person.

groups.name: Body destination versus receiving readiness
groups.statement: The contrast is between a bare bodily destination and an anticipatory receiving description such as waiting, outstretched, open, or awaiting.
groups.why: All members highlight readiness to receive, including hands, glove, or a waiting person, rather than only changing which body part is hit.

groups.name: Continued movement versus settling to rest
groups.statement: The contrast is between ongoing movement or routine continuation and sitting, settling, curling up, or otherwise coming to rest.
groups.why: All members share the same transition in activity state: ongoing motion versus rest.

groups.name: General emergency action versus emergency-specific response
groups.statement: The contrast is between broad action words and a more specified emergency-response repertoire including evacuate, escape, rescue, protect, or flee.
groups.why: The shared difference is specification of the response appropriate to the emergency, not a blanket change from movement to thought.

groups.name: Ingredient instance versus culinary category
groups.statement: The contrast is between specific ingredients and umbrella terms such as seasoning, ingredients, spices, or herbs.
groups.why: Both move between concrete instances and category-level ingredient descriptions, rather than between two individual seasonings.

groups.name: Enclosed destination versus open setting
groups.statement: The contrast is between enclosed, domestic, or private destinations and open, outdoor, or more publicly exposed settings.
groups.why: The recurrent spatial distinction is enclosure and privacy versus openness, with some overlapping or ambiguous destinations retained.

groups.name: Loose narrative continuation versus specified scene action
groups.statement: The contrast is between connectors, pronouns, or broad motion and more specified acts such as closing, locking, crossing, approaching, or entering.
groups.why: All members repeat the same action-specification contrast; they do not exclusively describe inner thought despite the labels.

groups.name: Action continuation versus path phrase
groups.statement: The contrast is between a new finite action or narrative continuation and a directional prepositional phrase such as into, onto, across, or toward.
groups.why: The shared change concerns grammatical continuation into a path, rather than choosing a different path endpoint.

groups.name: Specified date versus indefinite deferral
groups.statement: The contrast is between a named calendar date or day and an indefinite or relative postponement such as further, next, more, or later.
groups.why: Every member changes how definite the postponement endpoint is, not simply which date is selected.

groups.name: Water or broad landscape versus roadside features
groups.statement: The contrast is between water bodies or broad landscape destinations and near-road terrain such as ditches, bushes, embankments, medians, or hedges.
groups.why: The actual destination categories, rather than the readers’ distribution-narrowing labels, provide the shared movement.

groups.name: General body target versus catching apparatus
groups.statement: The contrast is between a range of body targets and a more specific receiving apparatus involving hand, hands, arm, mitt, or glove.
groups.why: A general bodily target and an apparatus for catching are the recurring alternatives; readiness modifiers accompany but do not define the entire contrast.
